title: Extreme Illuminated Vision Processing with a Graded Alloyed Perovskite In-sensor Computing Network

paper_content.abstract: In-sensor computing is proposed to reduce energy expenditure and processing latency by unifying sensing and computation within the hardware layer, yet the application under extreme illuminating scenario remains constrained by simultaneously obtaining broadband responsivity, large linear dynamic range and fast response. Here, we report a fully vapor-deposited graded Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite heterojunction photodiode with improved crystal quality. It enables the detection of light from visible to infrared light with a 230 dB linear dynamic range and 33 ns response time. We also develop a wafer-scale imaging processor by integrating the photodiode to a reconfigurable array. With this approach, we demonstrate biomedical detection and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding. The in-sensor processor realizes low-power high-resolution visible to infrared wavelength edge detection, adaptive background suppression under dim light and noise-immune high-speed dynamic imaging. Our results extend the options for in-sensor computing hardware, and thus pave a way toward practical artificial intelligent machine vision.
paper_content.introduction:
Traditional machine vision systems isolate sensing and processing units, incurring substantial energy consumption and latency from data transfer between image sensors and backend processors. This bottleneck hinders real-time applications in edge computing and artificial intelligence1,2. In-sensor or near-sensor computing addresses this by enabling pixel-level preprocessing before data transmission, necessitating in-situ reconfigurable photoresponsivity3,4. Recent advances leverage novel device architectures, including electrical doping5, ion migration6, ferroelectric effect7, float gating mechanism8, to dynamic reconfigure photoresponsivity. These approaches have demonstrated functionalities critical to machine vision, such as objection recognition9, motion perception5,10, high-speed data processing11, spectral extraction12, and in-sensor data compression13.

Practical application of in-sensor computing technology in machine vision, particularly for extreme illuminated conditions, however, remains a significant challenge, requiring the operation of photodiode with high speed, large dynamic range and extended wavelength12,14,15. Firstly, imaging under dim light or noisy environment is demanded yet difficult for a large number of important application context. Dealing with both weak and strong illuminated regions in a same image calls for sensors with a large linear dynamic range (LDR). Unfortunately, the LDR in most sensors is limited to no more than 150 dB, although a few work reported higher LDR by sacrificing the imaging speed16,17. Secondly, a neuromorphic visual system, such as for autonomous vehicles and robotics, needs to capture dynamic images. As a fundamental prerequisite, photodiode must have the operation speed down to nano-second level. However, response time is always compromised by power efficiency or detecting sensitivity. And finally, it is also necessary to expand the response to ultraviolet or infrared light, to capture information unavailable in the visible spectrum. For example, biomedical imaging is often operated at the infrared range.

Organic-inorganic hybrid perovskites, with high absorption coefficients and long carrier diffusion lengths, show great promise for optoelectronics. Recent advances have demonstrated the fabrication of thin film photodetector with better performance than crystalline Si18–21. Tin alloying narrows the bandgap and extends spectral responsivity into the near-infrared (NIR) while reducing lead base perovskite toxicity22,23. However, oxidation of Sn2+ to Sn4+ induces self p-doping and deep traps, elevating dark current and noise as well as undermining stability24. Even though sophisticated 2D/3D heterojunctions can partially suppress Sn2+ oxidation, the intrinsically low conductivity of 2D perovskites (~10−5 S cm−1) limits the photo-response efficiency25,26. Accordingly, realizing scalable, high quality, monolithically integratable perovskite units for practical in-sensor computing has remained as an open challenge.

Here, we introduce a gradient composition engineering strategy that provides a protective layer for oxidation suppression of Sn2+. By this approach, we fabricate stable lead-tin (Pb-Sn) alloyed perovskite films via fully vapor-deposition process. And based on these advancements, we demonstrate a scalable broadband bipolar programmable perovskite unit (BPPU). The core device comprises two sets of back-to-back cascaded perovskite photodiodes. This architecture enables rapid, stable, and precise control of photoresponse purely through circuit‑level biasing, avoiding trade‑offs in hysteresis, speed, or reliability. The uniform vapor-phase deposition ensures symmetric bipolar response tuning under low bias (±200 mV), fast response time of 33.0/37.4 ns and a large LDR of 230 dB. By integrating the BPPU into wafer-scale arrays, we achieve diverse in-sensor computing function such as adaptive background suppression, biomedical sensing and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding.
paper_content.results:
Design of Pb-Sn perovskite graded heterojunction photodiode
A fully vapor-deposition process is used for sequential layer-by-layer stacking of functional layers, which meets the requirements for future scalable, CMOS compatible and high-precision fabrication. The resulting device architecture is a vertical stacks of FTO/Spiro-TTB/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag (Fig. 1a).

High-quality Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite graded heterojunction is fabricated using a synergistic strategy combining compositional engineering and self-encapsulation as shown in Fig. 1b: First, co-evaporate SnI2 and PbI2 to form a homogeneous (SnI2:PbI2) mixing layer. Second, keep depositing PbI2 while shutting off the SnI2 source to deposit a thin pure PbI2 capping layer, forming a (SnI2:PbI2)/PbI2 heterojunction. The PbI2 capping layer acts as an encapsulation layer for the underlying SnI2. Finally, reacting the (SnI2:PbI2)/PbI2 heterojunction with vaporized methylamine iodide (MAI) at 180°C that converts it into MAPbxSn1-xI3/MAPbI3 perovskite thin film. Subsequent annealing, activate thermal diffusion promotes the crystallization and establishes a Pb-Sn ratio gradient across the film.

The effectiveness of the component engineering by the top PbI2 layer is supported by X-ray diffraction (XRD), optical absorption, and emission shifting in Supplementary Fig. 1 & Supplementary Fig. 2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis verifies PbI2 capping profoundly optimizes perovskite thin film morphology (Supplementary Fig. 3). While homogeneous structure perovskite films show a porous morphology with pinhole defects (Fig. 1c), introducing an 80 nm PbI2 capping layer on Pb-Sn alloyed precursor films yields dense perovskite grains with reduced inter crystalline voids (Fig. 1d). This microstructural densification decreases effectively suppressing leakage currents from 8.5×10−6 A to 5.6×10−8 A at −0.5 V bias for the device (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Effective prevention of Sn2+ oxidation in the graded structure is supported by the time evolution of photoluminescence (PL) (Fig. 1e-f, Supplementary Fig. 5). In homogeneous perovskite structure, the primary PL peak at 923 nm (Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite phase) suffers 50% intensity loss within 200 s (79% within 750 s), accompanied by an anomalous 702 nm emission peak emerging after 200 s—a signature of photoinduced Sn2+ oxidation forming MA2SnI6 phases27,28. In stark contrast, the sample pre-covered 80 nm PbI2 maintains >91% PL intensity of Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite over 750 s without secondary peak formation, demonstrating exceptional photostability. The effective encapsulation and protection of Sn2+ oxidation was further confirmed through femtosecond laser ablation XPS depth profiling of the aged samples (Supplementary Fig. 6). In devices characterization, devices based on the pre-covered 80 nm PbI2 layer show improved operational stability than the homogeneous control sample, with on-off switching characteristics remaining virtually unchanged after long-term continuous operation exceeding 700 hours (Supplementary Fig. 7) and demonstrating remarkable photostability even under strong light irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 8).

To verify the formation of compositional and band-structure gradient in the perovskite film, in-depth X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis is first employed, revealing Sn:Pb ratio evolves gradually from 0.05:0.95 at the surface to 0.4:0.6 in the bulk (Supplementary Fig. 9). Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measurement in Supplementary Fig. 10 is then employed to reveal the band structure, giving detail band alignment in Fig. 1g. It shows a type-II heterojunction between the Pb-Sn alloy region with band gap around 1.33 eV and Pb-rich surface layer with band gap around 1.50 eV. This continuous gradient results in a progressive spatial tilting of both the conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) across the entire active layer, effectively generating a built-in electric field. The Mott-Schottky analysis in Supplementary Fig. 11 further reveals an enhancement of built-in potential from 0.58 V in homogeneous film to 0.66 V in the gradient film. This built-in field actively drives photo-generated electrons towards the lead-rich region (orange arrow) and holes towards the tin-rich region (blue arrow) via directional drift, thereby transitioning carrier transport from diffusion-dominated to efficient drift-dominated. As a result, acceleration of charge separation and transport, substantially shortening carrier transit and residence time within the active layer can be expected. The observation of faster rise and fall times in the photoresponse of the graded heterojunction (Supplementary Fig. 12) provides evidence for the improved carrier transport kinetics.

The thickness of pre-covered PbI2 layer (Δ𝑑 = 20–110 nm) is a critical parameter for the compromise of device operational stability, carrier transport efficiency, and NIR sensitivity. The 80 nm PbI2 pre-covered layer provides an optimized NIR response. When the PbI2 thickness exceeds 80 nm, Pb-Sn balanced region which serves as the primary infrared absorber, is too short to preserve photo-response beyond 850 nm. This attenuation is directly evidenced by a 33% responsivity decrease at 850 nm in Δ𝑑 = 110 nm devices (0.28 A W−1 versus 0.42 A W−1 for 80 nm devices, Supplementary Fig. 13). Conversely, sub-80-nm pre-covered layers fail to adequately suppress oxidation-induced degradation, leading to deteriorated response. With the optimized structure, the gradient Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite film achieves a zero-bias external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 61.07% at 850 nm (Fig. 1h). This wavelength is crucial for NIR applications such as vein imaging that rely on the characteristic absorption of hemoglobin in the 760–850 nm spectral range. Although the PbI2 coating weakens the device’s short-wave infrared response above 850 nm, the high sensitivity maintained within the key spectral window fully meets the physical requirements of the targeted biomedical applications. This structure simultaneously satisfies essential intelligent vision system requirements including multi-wavelength adaptability, environmental stability, and rapid response capabilities.

Bipolar photoresponse perovskite in-sensor computing unit
In a machine vision system, the convolution of input optical signals and weights relies on a programmable photoresponse characteristics. As shown in the Fig. 2a, the designed BPPU integrates two vertically stacked photodiodes comprised of shared functional layer but adjacent electrically-isolated Ag electrodes. Detailed photocurrent-voltage characteristic of BPPU is shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. Fig. 2b shows the typical bias-dependent bipolar photoresponse that is understood by the equivalent circuit in the inset. Under uniform illumination intensity P, the photocurrent of BPPU is described by 𝐼total = 𝐼D1 + 𝐼D2. This relationship is verified by the photoresponse characteristic of individual photodiode by separately illuminating each diode. It’s found that the photodiode D1 contributed to the positive photoresponse and D2 contribute to the negative photoresponse. Fig. 2c maps the reconfigurable photoresponse as a function of incident power across a 400 mV window (−200 to +200 mV). The net responsivity can be continuously tuned from negative to positive. This enables optoelectronic analog multiplication and accumulation (MAC) for in-sensor computing applications (see below). Notably, the low operating voltage indicates the device is operated with ultra-low power consumption.

Building upon this back-to-back cascading configuration, leakage currents are self-cancelled as shown in Supplementary Fig. 15, suppressing the noise current to 7.44×10−14 A Hz−0.5 under 1 Hz as shown in Fig. 2d. The photodiode exhibits exceptional 230 dB LDR from 4.75 pW cm−2 to 1.50 W cm−2 under 860 nm in the BPPU at zero bias (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 16). Our device demonstrates competitive advantages over recently reported broadband (visible–NIR) photodetectors, as detailed in Supplementary Table 1. The BPPU achieves ultrafast bipolar photoresponse speed of 33.0 ns rise time and 37.4 ns fall time (Fig. 2f). It results from the cascaded architecture. The back-to-back connected diodes’ equivalent capacitance (𝐶eq = 𝐶1𝐶2 / (𝐶1+𝐶2)) reduces by 50% compared to single-photodiode configurations. The comparative data in Supplementary Fig. 17 provides direct experimental validation for this capacitance reduction effect.

This design establishes a new architecture for in-sensor computing devices, simultaneously addressing the longstanding trade-off between detection speed, sensitivity and power consumption in conventional photonic systems. Remarkably, our device accomplishes adjustable photo-response with an unprecedentedly low programming voltage of ±0.2 V – a figure significantly lower than state-of-the-art bipolar programmable photodetectors (Supplementary Table 2). The 230 dB dynamic range allows unified processing of vision with both low-light and high-flux parts without any gain switching/adapting. It overcomes the critical bottleneck of saturation-induced feature loss in existing neuromorphic vision sensors.

In-sensor computing core
Under zero bias, the BPPU readily functions as a computing kernel for hardware-level background (BG) suppression as demonstrated in Fig. 2g. The photocurrent fluctuations are constrained within <12.5 nA despite global BG illumination increasing from dark to 19.1 mW cm−2. This stability arises from responsivity cancellation (𝑅1 = −𝑅2) between neighboring diodes (D1 & D2 in Fig. 2b). It creates a hardware differential connection that effectively subtract the common-mode BG. But the total current is still able to sensitively response to locally illuminated signals. For example, a moving light spot induces negative (positive) signal when it goes through D1 (D2) zones. Our measurements suggest under dark BG, the array can resolve motion signal as dim as 146 pW (Fig. 2h). Even under a 42.18 mW intense BG illumination, a target signal down to 530 nW can be still successfully extracted from the strong BG (Fig. 2i), which corresponds to an interference level 98 dB stronger than the target signal. This robust performance is corroborated by the dynamic range measurements under strong background illumination (Supplementary Fig. 18). The BPPU achieves sub-microsecond fast BG suppression by directly performing analog photocurrent subtraction within the sensor hardware. This ability is not only promising for high-contrast scenes, but also bypassing conventional analog-to-digital conversion and digital signal processing. It definitely saves power and prevents precision loss. It is important to note that the excellent background suppression of the BPPU relies on uniform illumination across its two sub-pixels. In practical scenarios, spatial gradients or local shadows in back ground illumination may reduce the suppression efficiency and introduce low-frequency spatial artifacts. These effects can be mitigated by subsequent signal processing or system-level calibration strategies.

To further demonstrate the in-sensor computing capabilities, we also designed an extended BPPU array by integrating two fundamental units through a shared Ag current output terminal, as illustrated in Fig. 3a. Fig. 3b shows the equivalent circuit of this enhanced design. It provides independent bias terminals (𝑉A, 𝑉B) to program the responsivity of two branches and sum the photocurrent at the output terminal. Therefore, it is easy to understand each extended BPPU array serves as a minimum in-pixel MAC core for the input light intensity and weights defined by the bias voltage:
𝐼output = [𝑅(𝑉A),𝑅(𝑉B)] [𝑃A / 𝑃B] (1)

The MAC core can be further scaled up to form convolution kernel. We demonstrated a chip-level implementation of 2×2 and 6×6 extended BPPU arrays on a 4-inch wafer (Fig. 3c). Quantitative verification of film uniformity was achieved by measuring PL peak positions across 17 positions (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 19), revealing a standard deviation of only 2.21 nm. To further confirm the reliability of our deposition technique, the uniformity and reproducibility of the Sn/Pb gradient structure were assessed via XPS profiling, which shows high consistency over batches (Supplementary Fig. 20). Such exceptional homogeneity ensures high device-to-device consistency (Supplementary Fig. 21). The arrays can be programmed into any matrices for convolution operation. Fig. 3e&f give an instance. Base on the aforementioned reconfigurability, extensibility, and scalability, we next demonstrate the application of BPPU in intelligent vision tasks, from biomedical imaging/processing to real-time motion tracking.

In-sensor imaging processing for biomedical applications
BPPU based biological feature extraction was demonstrated using a home-built galvanometer-based scanner (Supplementary Fig. 22) for acquisition of both surface topography and subsurface vascular structures. For fingerprint biometrics, high-precision epidermal topography is captured under −0.2 V bias. It resolves ridge-valley structures (200–400 μm spacing) and sweat pore distributions (40–100 μm diameter, Fig. 4a). Switching to 0 V bias enables horizontal edge detection, where only the ridge boundaries are resolved as distinct intensity transitions (Fig. 4b) due to the differential output eliminated background signals. As shown in Fig. 4c, this operation manages to suppress nonlinear background variations and enables direct hardware-level extraction of Level 2 biometric features (bifurcations, ridge endings) and Level 3 identifiers (sweat pores)29,30. Notably, the resulting discretized edge map shows a 101% improvement in edge-specific signal-to-noise ratio, alongside 95.5% agreement with conventional digital processing outputs and higher contrast compared to conventional Sobel or Laplacian digital filters (Supplementary Fig. 23).

We also extended this in-sensor edge processing paradigm to deeper-tissue diagnostics through NIR absorption contrast. Hemoglobin in veins exhibits stronger absorption of NIR illumination than the surrounding tissues, such as skin and subcutaneous fat. NIR is thus very suitable for veins imaging. However, post-image processing techniques such as contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization and multi-scale filtering are required to address the weak contrast between the vein and surroundings tissue31–33. As shown in Fig. 4d, a photograph of a hand is provided with an inset highlighting the specific region used for imaging (Fig. 4e&f). A transmission image acquired using conventional imaging mode shows a high-intensity signal is detected between the fingers, while minimal venous detail is discernible (Fig. 4e), demonstrating the significant dynamic range challenge in conventional subcutaneous imaging. In contrast, under edge detection mode (Fig. 4f), the vein edges are clearly resolved due to abrupt transitions in hemoglobin concentration at vessel boundaries. This approach significantly enhances vein-to-tissue contrast, enabling clear visualization of vessels through differential absorption.

The device advantages for achieving this high quality image are two-fold. The intrinsically high LDR together with the differential architecture accommodate high-intensity background illumination from gap between fingers with tissue scattering and weak additive absorption signals from hemoglobin. Conventional photodetectors would otherwise saturate under high surface background intensity or lose vein-specific absorption variations in quantization noise. Consequently, the BPPU enables direct extraction of venous boundaries from raw NIR matrices without dynamic range compression. Notably, in contrast to conventional imaging with separate post-computation, our in-sensor computing approach operates at 0 V, approaching nearly zero-power data processing. Furthermore, the bipolar response characteristics of the extended BPPU array, in principle, allow it to be programmed to perform arbitrary two-dimensional linear convolution operations, effectively functioning as a versatile image processing kernel for various in-sensor computational imaging effects.

Beyond static in-sensor imaging application, the BPPU architecture also enables dynamic physiological monitoring through time-resolved differential sensing. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is a critical parameter for assessing arterial stiffness, which has been linked to various cardiovascular diseases34. Traditional PWV (𝑣) measurement requires multiple sensors and complex signal processing to analyze the time delay between pulse waves at different measurement sites35–37. However, this out- and multi-sensor data processing can be simplified by utilizing BPPU in-sensor computing. Here, we verify it through the local measurement of the fingers.

Fig. 4g schematically shows the in-sensor procession the photoplethysmographic (PPG) signal of when NIR light passes through tissues. The spatial separation (𝐷 = 2.5 mm) between the two sub-photodiodes introduces a small time lag (∆𝑇 = 𝐷/𝑣, typically < 0.5 ms for 𝑣 > 5 m s−1) in the pulse wave arriving times. This results in phase-shifted PPG signals (𝑃(𝑡) and 𝑃(𝑡−∆𝑇)) with distinct temporal characteristics. The BPPU computes the differential-delay current as 𝐼diff(𝑡) = 𝐼1(𝑡)−𝐼2(𝑡) = 𝛼[𝑃(𝑡)−𝑃(𝑡−∆𝑇)], where 𝛼 is the optoelectrical related coefficient. Since the ∆𝑇is significantly shorter than the PPG pulse wave’s characteristic timescale, the peak differential current at the maximum pulse slope ((d𝑃/d𝑡)max) is approximated by first-order Taylor expansion:

This yields the fundamental relationship of peak magnitude (𝐼diff,max) and PWV:
𝑣 = 𝑘 / 𝐼diff,max (3)

where the calibration constant 𝑘 = 𝛼 ∙𝐷(d𝑃/d𝑡)max incorporates optoelectronic and individual hemodynamic parameters. As experimentally confirmed in Fig. 4h, this inverse proportionality enables the direct translation of differential current peaks into PWV values. Fig. 4i demonstrates synchronized decreasing trends in both BPPU-derived normalized PWV and heart rate during post-exercise recovery. Physiological validation of our measurements is established through covariation with heart rate, which exhibits known correlation with PWV dynamics. Detailed signal processing is provided in Supplementary Fig. 24. Our approach thus enables efficient PWV monitoring through simple differential current measurement, offering a practical alternative to conventional multi-sensor systems.

Robust motion trajectory recognition
Finally, we use a dynamic spatiotemporal pattern recognition task to explore the potential of BPPU for intelligent vision. The task involves to identify the motion trajectory mode (32 kinds of distinct trajectories shown in Fig. 5a) of a specific target. The BPPU was scaled up to a 6×6 array. The trajectory-specific time-domain signals are generated via a convolution operation: 𝐼output(𝑡) = ∑𝑁𝑖=1 𝑅𝑖 𝜙𝑖(𝑡), where 𝑅 denotes the programmable responsivity of the 𝑖-th pixel (Fig. 3f, right), 𝜙 represents the time-dependent incident optical signal, and 𝑁 = 36 corresponds to the 6×6 array configuration. It enables the extended BPPU array directly encodes the moving objects’ spatiotemporal signatures into discriminative neuromorphic information. Or in other words, the BPPU sensor array naturally supports artificial neutral network vision processing as it played as the first layer of a neural network. The comprehensive system and detail recognition process are established in Supplementary Fig. 25 and Methods, and schematically illustrated in Fig. 5b. The original sensor output current for each BPPU in time-domain are shown in Fig. 5c & Supplementary Fig. 26. They were directly encoded into machine-readable features and sequentially fed into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for robust classification38,39. This workflow eliminates redundancy in conventional sensory systems (including data converters, digital edge detection, digital filtering, and optical flow calculation). Within the motion trajectory simulation platform measurements, the system achieves 100% classification accuracy across training, validation, and test sets (Fig. 5d) under noise-free conditions (Supplementary Fig. 27).

Robustness against noise is another main challenge for machine vision. We validate the system rigorous by examining its performance under perturbations. Specifically, we purposely introduced two distinct types of noise into the real trajectories: Gaussian noise and random walk noise. These were selected to simulate uncorrelated and temporally correlated interference common in real-world scenarios, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 28.

Fig. 5e summarizes the identification accuracy for signals subjected to single kind of noises. The Gaussian noise in our experiments models common uncorrelated, high-frequency disturbances in real-world scenarios, such as electronic readout noise in sensors and circuits as well as photon shot noise, which independently affects each measurement point. In this case, the system demonstrates exceptional resilience: test accuracy maintains 95.32% at 20% noise intensity, representing a marginal 4.68% degradation from baseline. This robustness stems from the uncorrelated nature of gaussian noise. The BPPU based system can effectively filter out this kind of transient perturbation. The random walk noise is selected to simulate cumulative, low-frequency interference, including mechanical drift or vibration and slow sensor baseline drift. Its accumulated effect introduces time-correlated deviations that distort the intended motion trajectory, thereby testing the system’s robustness against shape errors. These disturbances alter key shape features of the path and increase classification complexity. Nevertheless, the system maintains a test accuracy registers at 99.19% for 4% noise intensity and remains measurable at 81.71% under 20% intensity. This performance demonstrates robust tolerance to trajectory distortions.

And finally, we also performed a comprehensive evaluation by integrated training across all noise types and intensities, it yields a 90.87% classification accuracy (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Fig. 29). These results confirm the system’s robust discrimination capability, even for perceptually similar motion patterns under challenging conditions. Fundamentally limited by a 33‑ns temporal resolution, the BPPU-based system can directly encode fast motion. The corresponding theoretical maximum detectable velocity of 7.6×104 m s−1 (discussed in Supplementary Fig. 30), allowing the system to capture and classify rapid trajectories that would otherwise be blurred or missed by standard imaging systems.
paper_content.methods:
Materials
FTO glasses, Lead (II) iodide (PbI2), 2,2’7,7’tetra(N,N-di-tolyl)amino-9,9-spiro-bifluorene (Spiro-TTB) and C60 were purchased from Advanced Election Technology CO., Ltd. Tin (II) iodide SnI2 (99.999%) was purchased from 3AMaterials. Methylammonium iodide (CH3NH3I, MAI) (99.8%) was purchased from TCI. 2,9-dimethyl-4,7-diphenyl-1,10-phenanthroline (BCP) were purchased from Xi’an Polymer Light Technology Corp. All of the chemicals were used as received.

Perovskite photodiode and BPPU fabrication
The device structure was configured with a vertically stacked structure. Prepatterned FTO substrates were cleaned, treated with oxygen plasma, and then deposited with a 6 nm Spiro-TTB layer via thermal evaporation (~0.1 Å s−1). The graded perovskite heterojunction was fabricated through a sequential vapor-deposition process wherein SnI2 and PbI2 were first co-evaporated at a 1:1 molar ratio to form a homogeneous underlying layer with a total fixed thickness of 180 nm. The SnI2 source was then terminated at a stage corresponding to a PbI2 capping thickness (varied from 0 to 110 nm), depositing a pure PbI2 overlayer. Finally, the stacked precursor film was converted into a compositionally graded perovskite structure via reaction with vaporized MAI in a 180 °C vacuum oven. After cooling, the perovskite film was IPA-spin cleaned and annealed (100 °C, 10 min). Subsequent layers included thermally evaporated C60 (23 nm, ~0.1 Å s−1) and BCP (8 nm, ~0.08 Å s−1). The Ag electrode was finally deposited by thermal evaporation through a patterned shadow mask. For optoelectronic characterization, imaging, and trajectory recognition, the sub-photodiode areas of the BPPUs are 0.04 cm2, 4×10−4 cm2, and 0.01 cm2, respectively.

Film characterization
Ultraviolet-visible absorption spectra were measured using SHIMADZU UV-2600. The PL spectrum was measured using confocal Raman microscope (WITec, Alpha300R) with a 532 nm laser as the excitation source. SEM images were acquired through a FEI Quanta 450 FEG field emission scanning electron microscope. XRD spectra were acquired using a BRUKER D8-Advance equipped with Cu K𝛼1 irradiation (𝜆 = 1.5406 Å). UPS characterizations were performed using with a Thermo Fisher Scientific K-Alpha+ equipped with a He I (21.22 eV) excitation source. XPS for Pb-Sn ratio characterizations were acquired on the same instrument (Al Kα radiation source). Femtosecond laser ablation (fs-LA) XPS depth profiling for Sn2+ oxidation analysis was performed using a Thermo Fisher Scientific Hypulse XPS system40,41. Single femtosecond laser pulses of 40 μJ per level were employed, delivered as a horizontally linearly polarized Gaussian beam with a wavelength of 1030 nm and a pulse duration of 160 fs.

Device characterization
The electrical characterization of the photodiode and BPPU devices was conducted in a dark metal box to avoid interference from ambient light. Current-voltage characteristics were measured using a source-measure unit (Keithley 2612A Source Meters).

The LDR measurement was referred to the methodology outlined in the literature42,43. The device was illuminated by a modulated laser and the resulting photocurrent was detected with a lock‑in amplifier (Guangzhou Sine Scientific Instrument Co., LTD, Model OE2031) under zero bias. The frequency spectral response was obtained by scanning the reference frequency and standardized according to the equivalent noise bandwidth determined by the lock-in amplifier’s filter order and time constant. During the experiment, the incident optical power was calibrated with an optical power meter (Daheng Optics, GCI-080302) and attenuated using a series of neutral density filters (Thorlabs).

Noise current measurements were conducted at room temperature under dark condition, also utilizing the lock-in amplifier. EQE spectra were acquired at zero bias using an Enlitech QE-C system. The response time was acquired by an oscilloscope (Tektronix, TDS2024C) through a trans-impedance amplifier.

The BPPU array was tested using a home-built multi-channel scanning system. A Keithley 3706A Switch/Multimeter with a plug-in card (Keithley 3730 matrix card) was used to select rows and columns to determine the read-out terminal to be tested.

Imaging processing demonstration
Our home-built galvanometer scanning imager utilizes dual-axis galvanometer driven by XY-voltage inputs for rapid predefined trajectory scanning. The system directs reflected or transmitted scene light through a camera lens onto the photodetector. Real-time voltage programming dynamically reconfigures BPPU’s image processing functions, with processed signals acquired via TIA and lock-in amplification for subsequent image reconstruction.

Motion trajectory experimental platform
An 850 nm laser serves as the light source, with its beam dynamically steered across the BPPU device following a preset trajectory via a dual-axis galvanometer scanner. The multi-channel digital-to-analog converter provides 18 independent biases, pre-programming the 6×6 BPPU array to the target response matrix. A TIA and a lock-in amplifier used to acquire the resulting time-series current signals generated by the BPPU under dynamic laser spot stimulation.

The acquired noise-free trajectories and with-noise variants were used to construct different datasets. For evaluating the impact of each noise intensity level, a dedicated dataset was assembled per intensity, consisting of 256 noise-free samples and 320 with-noise variants samples, yielding 576 samples in total. For the comprehensive evaluation involving integrated training across all noise types and intensities, a combined dataset was created by merging the noise-free data with all noisy samples, resulting in 3,232 samples in total. The BPPU generated time-series features were fed into an LSTM network comprising a 128 hidden units LSTM layer, a fully connected layer, and a softmax output layer, which was trained with the Adam optimizer (initial learning rate: 0.001) for up to 100 epochs.

variation contribute to device performance?

under high light intensity backgrounds. Please provide data on the device's performance under strong light backgrounds and
discuss its stability, particularly focusing on dynamic range and saturation behavior under these conditions.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This paper presents a graded Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite heterojunction photodiode fabricated via a full vapor deposition
process, achieving broadband response from visible to infrared, an ultra-large linear dynamic range of 238 dB, and a fast
response time of 33 ns. The authors further develop a wafer-scale in-sensor computing network, demonstrating its
application in biomedical imaging and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding. The work is highly compelling, showcasing
significant advancements in material design, device performance, and system integration for intelligent machine vision. It is
recommended that the authors address the points raised below to further strengthen the manuscript.
1. The manuscript contains several instances of non-standard unit formatting. For example, in line 151, a space is missing
between the numerical value and its unit.
2. While XPS/UPS data confirm a Sn/Pb gradient in a localized area, the uniformity and reproducibility of this gradient
across the entire wafer scale remain unverified. To robustly demonstrate the controllability of this deposition process for
scalable manufacturing, please provide additional data.
3. The PL stability data indirectly suggest suppressed Sn2+ oxidation. To provide direct chemical evidence, I recommend
comparing the Sn 3d XPS spectra, including depth profiling, of the homogeneous and graded heterojunction films before
and after aging. This would visually demonstrate the effective suppression of Sn4+ formation in the graded structure.
4. The 700-hour operational stability test shown in Fig. S6 is a key result. However, the critical parameters of the optical
stimulus used for the "on-off switching" test are not specified . Please provide these details. In addition, is there a difference
in the durability of devices under different light intensity stimuli?
5. In Figure 2a, the labels for the material layers in the device structure are missing.
6. To unequivocally verify that the noise reduction stems from correlated noise common-mode rejection in the back-to-back
configuration—rather than inherently low noise in each individual photodiode—please provide the independent noise
current spectra for both sub-photodiodes (D1 and D2) measured at zero bias.
7. The reported ultra-fast response time (33 ns) is remarkable. Please specify the intensity of the optical pulse used in this
measurement.
8. The authors’ explanation that the speed improvement arises from the reduced effective capacitance in the back-to-back
structure is theoretically reliable. However, in addition to this theoretical interpretation, the response speed of a single device
should also be measured and compared with that of the composite structure to provide practical verification.
9. When the background illumination incident on the sensor array is not perfectly uniform (for example, when gradients or
localized shadows are present), D1 and D2 will experience different light intensities. Could this lead to a degradation of the
background-suppression effect, or even generate spurious signals?
10. The manuscript reports an ultrahigh linear dynamic range of 238 dB together with a zero-bias EQE of ~61% at 850 nm,
which is an excellent performance combination. To conclusively demonstrate that the photoresponse remains linear across
the entire dynamic range, and that the high EQE is not limited to a specific illumination level, please provide EQE curves
measured under varying incident light intensities.

Dear Reviewers,

Nature Communications. We deeply appreciate your constructive and encouraging comments. After a
careful consideration all these questions and suggestions, we have revised the manuscript and compiled
a detailed point-by-point response as follows.
This work reports a graded Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite heterojunction photodiode fabricated via vapor
deposition, which is then used to construct a bipolar programmable unit and an in-sense computing
network. The research successfully addresses the classic challenge in high-performance photodetectors
of simultaneously achieving broadband response, large linear dynamic range, and fast response speed.
More importantly, the authors go beyond a simple device performance demonstration by tightly
integrating device innovation with system-level applications, showcasing a series of cutting-edge in-
sensor computing applications ranging from biomedical imaging to robust motion trajectory
recognition. Overall, this is an outstanding and impressive piece of work, paving a new way for
perovskite applications in next-generation machine vision. I would like to recommend this manuscript
for publication in Nature Communications. Here are some specific comments and suggestions:
1. The introduction cites numerous works utilizing novel physical mechanisms (e.g., ion migration,
ferroelectric effect) to achieve programmable photoresponse. Please further clarify whether the core
innovation of the proposed BPPU architecture stems from a breakthrough in device physics or from
an ingenious circuit architecture combination? How does it fundamentally differ from the mechanisms
in the cited literature?
Reply:
Thank you for raising this important question regarding the core innovation of our BPPU architecture.
We appreciate the opportunity to clarify that the novelty lies not in the discovery of a new physical
mechanism, but in the synergistic integration of a stable material innovation with an ingenious circuit
architecture to achieve robust and programmable in-sensor computing. Below we detail the respective
contributions and the fundamental distinction from the mechanisms cited in the introduction.
(1) Device-Level Innovation: The foundation of this work is the gradient Pb–Sn alloyed perovskite
heterojunction fabricated via a fully vapor-phase process. This gradient structure constitutes a
material and device innovation by effectively suppressing Sn2+ oxidation and substantially
enhancing operational stability. Moreover, its built-in bandgap gradient promotes the efficient and
rapid extraction of photogenerated carriers. This graded heterojunction provides the essential
2
material basis for the BPPU’s broadband response, large LDR, and fast response speed.
Furthermore, the vapor-phase process ensures excellent device-to-device uniformity, which is
critical for enabling the subsequent circuit-level functionality based on differential detection.
(2) Circuit-Architecture Innovation: The programmability and bipolar photoresponse of the BPPU are
achieved through its back-to-back dual photodiode configuration with independent bias control
(V , V ). By electrically tuning the biases applied to the two photodiodes, we can precisely and
A B
rapidly control the net photoresponse (both polarity and amplitude). This architecture leverages the
symmetry of two well-matched photodiodes to enable, at zero net bias: (a) Common-mode
rejection of correlated background/noise; (b) Reduced effective capacitance, resulting in ultrafast
response speed.
In contrast to the mechanisms referenced in the introduction (e.g., ion migration, ferroelectric effects),
which modulate photoresponse by altering the intrinsic properties of the semiconductor material itself,
the BPPU employs a pair of stable, fixed-characteristic photodiodes. Its programmability is achieved
through electrical control at the architectural level via external circuit biases. This approach avoids
herent drawbacks associated with material-property switching, such as hysteresis, slow speed, or
reliability degradation, thereby offering a more generalizable and robust pathway for fast, stable, and
precise programmable photoelectric computing.
We have supplemented the Introduction sections to more explicitly articulate this distinction (Page 4).
“Here, we introduce a gradient composition engineering strategy that provides a protective layer for
oxidation suppression of Sn2+. By this approach, we fabricate stable lead-tin (Pb-Sn) alloyed perovskite
films via fully vapor deposition process. And based on these advancements, we demonstrate a scalable
broadband perovskite bipolar programmable unit (BPPU). The core device comprises two sets of back-
to-back cascaded perovskite photodiodes. This architecture enables rapid, stable, and precise control
of photoresponse purely through circuit‑level biasing, avoiding trade‑offs in hysteresis, speed, or
reliability. The uniform vapor-phase deposition ensures symmetric bipolar response tuning under low
bias (±200 mV), fast response time of 33.0/37.4 ns and a large LDR of 230 dB. By integrating the
BPPU into wafer-scale arrays, we achieve diverse in-sensor computing function such as adaptive
background suppression, biomedical sensing and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding.”

short-wave infrared response, and analyze if this is acceptable for target applications like vein imaging.

~900 nm compared to a uniform Pb-Sn perovskite of equivalent total thickness.
This trade-off, however, is acceptable and indeed beneficial for our target application of vein imaging.
The key physiological contrast for vein imaging relies on the characteristic absorption of hemoglobin
within the 760–850 nm spectral range. Crucially, our optimized graded heterojunction maintains an
external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 61.07% at 850 nm (Fig. 1h), ensuring sufficient sensitivity
across this critical window. This practical efficacy is directly demonstrated by our finger vein imaging
experiments, which successfully captured clear venous networks (Fig. 4d–f).
The overall benefits provided by the graded structure, including the improvement in operational
stability, significant suppression of dark current, and optimized charge extraction efficiency, far
outweigh the marginal loss in SWIR response beyond the primary spectral region of interest. Therefore,
this design compromise remains highly advantageous for building a stable and practical visible-to-NIR
vision system.

Thank you for your insightful questions regarding the Sn/Pb gradient. The compositional gradient
observed in our devices, particularly the variation of the Sn to Pb ratio with depth, indeed primarily
stems from our meticulously designed two-step vapor deposition process. This process, along with
subsequent thermal treatments, is crucial for achieving this finely tuned gradient structure.
First, during our initial vapor deposition step, we co-evaporate SnI and PbI onto the substrate. This

What truly transforms this stepped structure into a smooth gradient is the subsequent reaction and
thermal treatment process, the reaction with methylammonium iodide (MAI) vapor and the crucial
180°C thermal annealing. Under elevated temperatures, thermally activated interlayer diffusion
becomes highly significant. Sn and Pb ions begin to migrate between the two layers. Owing to the
initial concentration differences and the intrinsic diffusion dynamics of these ions within the perovskite
lattice, this process smooths out the initially abrupt compositional distribution. Within the limited
annealing time and temperature, continuous ion exchange and diffusion ultimately establish a
continuous gradient, leading to a Pb-rich surface region and a gradual increase in tin content with depth
into the film, thereby forming the Sn/Pb gradient distribution with a Pb-rich surface as shown in Fig
S9.
Optically, this meticulously crafted Pb/Sn gradient establishes a continuous bandgap variation across
the perovskite film in the vertical direction, ranging from approximately 1.33 eV at the bottom to 1.50
eV at the surface. Concomitantly, this gradual change in bandgap is inherently accompanied by a
refractive index gradient. As light enters the material from the air, this smooth transition in refractive
index effectively minimizes reflection losses at the interface, thereby ensuring efficient broadband
absorption from the visible to the near-infrared spectrum. These profound optical enhancements lay a
crucial foundation for subsequent efficient charge separation and collection.
Electrically, as mentioned in the previous comments, the gradient bandgap profile creates a powerful
built-in electric field extending across the perovskite layer. This intrinsic electric field is critical for
facilitating highly efficient, drift-dominated transport of photogenerated carriers. It effectively guides
electrons and holes towards their respective selective transport layers, significantly accelerating their
separation and transport. This rapid carrier movement profoundly reduces the overall carrier transit

time within the device, thereby substantially boosting the intrinsic mobility of the entire perovskite
film.
The synergistic interplay of these optical and electrical improvements directly translates into enhanced
overall device performance. Specifically, the gradient structure ensures a high EQE, particularly in the
near-infrared region, by optimizing light capture and utilization. Furthermore, the significantly
improved carrier transport underpins a remarkably faster device response. Crucially, the inherent
design of this gradient features a dense Pb-rich surface layer (effectively acting as encapsulation),
plays a vital role in mitigating the degradation of Sn2+ from exposure and oxidation, thereby ensuring
the device’s excellent long-term stability.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

In-sensor computing is proposed to reduce energy expenditure and processing latency by unifying sensing and computation within the hardware layer, yet the application under extreme illuminating scenario remains constrained by simultaneously obtaining broadband responsivity, large linear dynamic range and fast response. Here, we report a fully vapor-deposited graded Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite heterojunction photodiode with improved crystal quality. It enables the detection of light from visible to infrared light with a 230 dB linear dynamic range and 33 ns response time. We also develop a wafer-scale imaging processor by integrating the photodiode to a reconfigurable array. With this approach, we demonstrate biomedical detection and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding. The in-sensor processor realizes low-power high-resolution visible to infrared wavelength edge detection, adaptive background suppression under dim light and noise-immune high-speed dynamic imaging. Our results extend the options for in-sensor computing hardware, and thus pave a way toward practical artificial intelligent machine vision.

---

## Introduction

Traditional machine vision systems isolate sensing and processing units, incurring substantial energy consumption and latency from data transfer between image sensors and backend processors. This bottleneck hinders real-time applications in edge computing and artificial intelligence1,2. In-sensor or near-sensor computing addresses this by enabling pixel-level preprocessing before data transmission, necessitating in-situ reconfigurable photoresponsivity3,4. Recent advances leverage novel device architectures, including electrical doping5, ion migration6, ferroelectric effect7, float gating mechanism8, to dynamic reconfigure photoresponsivity. These approaches have demonstrated functionalities critical to machine vision, such as objection recognition9, motion perception5,10, high-speed data processing11, spectral extraction12, and in-sensor data compression13.

Practical application of in-sensor computing technology in machine vision, particularly for extreme illuminated conditions, however, remains a significant challenge, requiring the operation of photodiode with high speed, large dynamic range and extended wavelength12,14,15. Firstly, imaging under dim light or noisy environment is demanded yet difficult for a large number of important application context. Dealing with both weak and strong illuminated regions in a same image calls for sensors with a large linear dynamic range (LDR). Unfortunately, the LDR in most sensors is limited to no more than 150 dB, although a few work reported higher LDR by sacrificing the imaging speed16,17. Secondly, a neuromorphic visual system, such as for autonomous vehicles and robotics, needs to capture dynamic images. As a fundamental prerequisite, photodiode must have the operation speed down to nano-second level. However, response time is always compromised by power efficiency or detecting sensitivity. And finally, it is also necessary to expand the response to ultraviolet or infrared light, to capture information unavailable in the visible spectrum. For example, biomedical imaging is often operated at the infrared range.

Organic-inorganic hybrid perovskites, with high absorption coefficients and long carrier diffusion lengths, show great promise for optoelectronics. Recent advances have demonstrated the fabrication of thin film photodetector with better performance than crystalline Si18–21. Tin alloying narrows the bandgap and extends spectral responsivity into the near-infrared (NIR) while reducing lead base perovskite toxicity22,23. However, oxidation of Sn2+ to Sn4+ induces self p-doping and deep traps, elevating dark current and noise as well as undermining stability24. Even though sophisticated 2D/3D heterojunctions can partially suppress Sn2+ oxidation, the intrinsically low conductivity of 2D perovskites (~10−5 S cm−1) limits the photo-response efficiency25,26. Accordingly, realizing scalable, high quality, monolithically integratable perovskite units for practical in-sensor computing has remained as an open challenge.

Here, we introduce a gradient composition engineering strategy that provides a protective layer for oxidation suppression of Sn2+. By this approach, we fabricate stable lead-tin (Pb-Sn) alloyed perovskite films via fully vapor-deposition process. And based on these advancements, we demonstrate a scalable broadband bipolar programmable perovskite unit (BPPU). The core device comprises two sets of back-to-back cascaded perovskite photodiodes. This architecture enables rapid, stable, and precise control of photoresponse purely through circuit‑level biasing, avoiding trade‑offs in hysteresis, speed, or reliability. The uniform vapor-phase deposition ensures symmetric bipolar response tuning under low bias (±200 mV), fast response time of 33.0/37.4 ns and a large LDR of 230 dB. By integrating the BPPU into wafer-scale arrays, we achieve diverse in-sensor computing function such as adaptive background suppression, biomedical sensing and spatiotemporal trajectory encoding.

---

## Results

Design of Pb-Sn perovskite graded heterojunction photodiode
A fully vapor-deposition process is used for sequential layer-by-layer stacking of functional layers, which meets the requirements for future scalable, CMOS compatible and high-precision fabrication. The resulting device architecture is a vertical stacks of FTO/Spiro-TTB/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag (Fig. 1a).

High-quality Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite graded heterojunction is fabricated using a synergistic strategy combining compositional engineering and self-encapsulation as shown in Fig. 1b: First, co-evaporate SnI2 and PbI2 to form a homogeneous (SnI2:PbI2) mixing layer. Second, keep depositing PbI2 while shutting off the SnI2 source to deposit a thin pure PbI2 capping layer, forming a (SnI2:PbI2)/PbI2 heterojunction. The PbI2 capping layer acts as an encapsulation layer for the underlying SnI2. Finally, reacting the (SnI2:PbI2)/PbI2 heterojunction with vaporized methylamine iodide (MAI) at 180°C that converts it into MAPbxSn1-xI3/MAPbI3 perovskite thin film. Subsequent annealing, activate thermal diffusion promotes the crystallization and establishes a Pb-Sn ratio gradient across the film.

The effectiveness of the component engineering by the top PbI2 layer is supported by X-ray diffraction (XRD), optical absorption, and emission shifting in Supplementary Fig. 1 & Supplementary Fig. 2. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis verifies PbI2 capping profoundly optimizes perovskite thin film morphology (Supplementary Fig. 3). While homogeneous structure perovskite films show a porous morphology with pinhole defects (Fig. 1c), introducing an 80 nm PbI2 capping layer on Pb-Sn alloyed precursor films yields dense perovskite grains with reduced inter crystalline voids (Fig. 1d). This microstructural densification decreases effectively suppressing leakage currents from 8.5×10−6 A to 5.6×10−8 A at −0.5 V bias for the device (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Effective prevention of Sn2+ oxidation in the graded structure is supported by the time evolution of photoluminescence (PL) (Fig. 1e-f, Supplementary Fig. 5). In homogeneous perovskite structure, the primary PL peak at 923 nm (Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite phase) suffers 50% intensity loss within 200 s (79% within 750 s), accompanied by an anomalous 702 nm emission peak emerging after 200 s—a signature of photoinduced Sn2+ oxidation forming MA2SnI6 phases27,28. In stark contrast, the sample pre-covered 80 nm PbI2 maintains >91% PL intensity of Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite over 750 s without secondary peak formation, demonstrating exceptional photostability. The effective encapsulation and protection of Sn2+ oxidation was further confirmed through femtosecond laser ablation XPS depth profiling of the aged samples (Supplementary Fig. 6). In devices characterization, devices based on the pre-covered 80 nm PbI2 layer show improved operational stability than the homogeneous control sample, with on-off switching characteristics remaining virtually unchanged after long-term continuous operation exceeding 700 hours (Supplementary Fig. 7) and demonstrating remarkable photostability even under strong light irradiation (Supplementary Fig. 8).

To verify the formation of compositional and band-structure gradient in the perovskite film, in-depth X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis is first employed, revealing Sn:Pb ratio evolves gradually from 0.05:0.95 at the surface to 0.4:0.6 in the bulk (Supplementary Fig. 9). Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) measurement in Supplementary Fig. 10 is then employed to reveal the band structure, giving detail band alignment in Fig. 1g. It shows a type-II heterojunction between the Pb-Sn alloy region with band gap around 1.33 eV and Pb-rich surface layer with band gap around 1.50 eV. This continuous gradient results in a progressive spatial tilting of both the conduction band minimum (CBM) and valence band maximum (VBM) across the entire active layer, effectively generating a built-in electric field. The Mott-Schottky analysis in Supplementary Fig. 11 further reveals an enhancement of built-in potential from 0.58 V in homogeneous film to 0.66 V in the gradient film. This built-in field actively drives photo-generated electrons towards the lead-rich region (orange arrow) and holes towards the tin-rich region (blue arrow) via directional drift, thereby transitioning carrier transport from diffusion-dominated to efficient drift-dominated. As a result, acceleration of charge separation and transport, substantially shortening carrier transit and residence time within the active layer can be expected. The observation of faster rise and fall times in the photoresponse of the graded heterojunction (Supplementary Fig. 12) provides evidence for the improved carrier transport kinetics.

The thickness of pre-covered PbI2 layer (Δ𝑑 = 20–110 nm) is a critical parameter for the compromise of device operational stability, carrier transport efficiency, and NIR sensitivity. The 80 nm PbI2 pre-covered layer provides an optimized NIR response. When the PbI2 thickness exceeds 80 nm, Pb-Sn balanced region which serves as the primary infrared absorber, is too short to preserve photo-response beyond 850 nm. This attenuation is directly evidenced by a 33% responsivity decrease at 850 nm in Δ𝑑 = 110 nm devices (0.28 A W−1 versus 0.42 A W−1 for 80 nm devices, Supplementary Fig. 13). Conversely, sub-80-nm pre-covered layers fail to adequately suppress oxidation-induced degradation, leading to deteriorated response. With the optimized structure, the gradient Pb-Sn alloyed perovskite film achieves a zero-bias external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 61.07% at 850 nm (Fig. 1h). This wavelength is crucial for NIR applications such as vein imaging that rely on the characteristic absorption of hemoglobin in the 760–850 nm spectral range. Although the PbI2 coating weakens the device’s short-wave infrared response above 850 nm, the high sensitivity maintained within the key spectral window fully meets the physical requirements of the targeted biomedical applications. This structure simultaneously satisfies essential intelligent vision system requirements including multi-wavelength adaptability, environmental stability, and rapid response capabilities.

Bipolar photoresponse perovskite in-sensor computing unit
In a machine vision system, the convolution of input optical signals and weights relies on a programmable photoresponse characteristics. As shown in the Fig. 2a, the designed BPPU integrates two vertically stacked photodiodes comprised of shared functional layer but adjacent electrically-isolated Ag electrodes. Detailed photocurrent-voltage characteristic of BPPU is shown in Supplementary Fig. 14. Fig. 2b shows the typical bias-dependent bipolar photoresponse that is understood by the equivalent circuit in the inset. Under uniform illumination intensity P, the photocurrent of BPPU is described by 𝐼total = 𝐼D1 + 𝐼D2. This relationship is verified by the photoresponse characteristic of individual photodiode by separately illuminating each diode. It’s found that the photodiode D1 contributed to the positive photoresponse and D2 contribute to the negative photoresponse. Fig. 2c maps the reconfigurable photoresponse as a function of incident power across a 400 mV window (−200 to +200 mV). The net responsivity can be continuously tuned from negative to positive. This enables optoelectronic analog multiplication and accumulation (MAC) for in-sensor computing applications (see below). Notably, the low operating voltage indicates the device is operated with ultra-low power consumption.

Building upon this back-to-back cascading configuration, leakage currents are self-cancelled as shown in Supplementary Fig. 15, suppressing the noise current to 7.44×10−14 A Hz−0.5 under 1 Hz as shown in Fig. 2d. The photodiode exhibits exceptional 230 dB LDR from 4.75 pW cm−2 to 1.50 W cm−2 under 860 nm in the BPPU at zero bias (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 16). Our device demonstrates competitive advantages over recently reported broadband (visible–NIR) photodetectors, as detailed in Supplementary Table 1. The BPPU achieves ultrafast bipolar photoresponse speed of 33.0 ns rise time and 37.4 ns fall time (Fig. 2f). It results from the cascaded architecture. The back-to-back connected diodes’ equivalent capacitance (𝐶eq = 𝐶1𝐶2 / (𝐶1+𝐶2)) reduces by 50% compared to single-photodiode configurations. The comparative data in Supplementary Fig. 17 provides direct experimental validation for this capacitance reduction effect.

This design establishes a new architecture for in-sensor computing devices, simultaneously addressing the longstanding trade-off between detection speed, sensitivity and power consumption in conventional photonic systems. Remarkably, our device accomplishes adjustable photo-response with an unprecedentedly low programming voltage of ±0.2 V – a figure significantly lower than state-of-the-art bipolar programmable photodetectors (Supplementary Table 2). The 230 dB dynamic range allows unified processing of vision with both low-light and high-flux parts without any gain switching/adapting. It overcomes the critical bottleneck of saturation-induced feature loss in existing neuromorphic vision sensors.

In-sensor computing core
Under zero bias, the BPPU readily functions as a computing kernel for hardware-level background (BG) suppression as demonstrated in Fig. 2g. The photocurrent fluctuations are constrained within <12.5 nA despite global BG illumination increasing from dark to 19.1 mW cm−2. This stability arises from responsivity cancellation (𝑅1 = −𝑅2) between neighboring diodes (D1 & D2 in Fig. 2b). It creates a hardware differential connection that effectively subtract the common-mode BG. But the total current is still able to sensitively response to locally illuminated signals. For example, a moving light spot induces negative (positive) signal when it goes through D1 (D2) zones. Our measurements suggest under dark BG, the array can resolve motion signal as dim as 146 pW (Fig. 2h). Even under a 42.18 mW intense BG illumination, a target signal down to 530 nW can be still successfully extracted from the strong BG (Fig. 2i), which corresponds to an interference level 98 dB stronger than the target signal. This robust performance is corroborated by the dynamic range measurements under strong background illumination (Supplementary Fig. 18). The BPPU achieves sub-microsecond fast BG suppression by directly performing analog photocurrent subtraction within the sensor hardware. This ability is not only promising for high-contrast scenes, but also bypassing conventional analog-to-digital conversion and digital signal processing. It definitely saves power and prevents precision loss. It is important to note that the excellent background suppression of the BPPU relies on uniform illumination across its two sub-pixels. In practical scenarios, spatial gradients or local shadows in back ground illumination may reduce the suppression efficiency and introduce low-frequency spatial artifacts. These effects can be mitigated by subsequent signal processing or system-level calibration strategies.

To further demonstrate the in-sensor computing capabilities, we also designed an extended BPPU array by integrating two fundamental units through a shared Ag current output terminal, as illustrated in Fig. 3a. Fig. 3b shows the equivalent circuit of this enhanced design. It provides independent bias terminals (𝑉A, 𝑉B) to program the responsivity of two branches and sum the photocurrent at the output terminal. Therefore, it is easy to understand each extended BPPU array serves as a minimum in-pixel MAC core for the input light intensity and weights defined by the bias voltage:
𝐼output = [𝑅(𝑉A),𝑅(𝑉B)] [𝑃A / 𝑃B] (1)

The MAC core can be further scaled up to form convolution kernel. We demonstrated a chip-level implementation of 2×2 and 6×6 extended BPPU arrays on a 4-inch wafer (Fig. 3c). Quantitative verification of film uniformity was achieved by measuring PL peak positions across 17 positions (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 19), revealing a standard deviation of only 2.21 nm. To further confirm the reliability of our deposition technique, the uniformity and reproducibility of the Sn/Pb gradient structure were assessed via XPS profiling, which shows high consistency over batches (Supplementary Fig. 20). Such exceptional homogeneity ensures high device-to-device consistency (Supplementary Fig. 21). The arrays can be programmed into any matrices for convolution operation. Fig. 3e&f give an instance. Base on the aforementioned reconfigurability, extensibility, and scalability, we next demonstrate the application of BPPU in intelligent vision tasks, from biomedical imaging/processing to real-time motion tracking.

In-sensor imaging processing for biomedical applications
BPPU based biological feature extraction was demonstrated using a home-built galvanometer-based scanner (Supplementary Fig. 22) for acquisition of both surface topography and subsurface vascular structures. For fingerprint biometrics, high-precision epidermal topography is captured under −0.2 V bias. It resolves ridge-valley structures (200–400 μm spacing) and sweat pore distributions (40–100 μm diameter, Fig. 4a). Switching to 0 V bias enables horizontal edge detection, where only the ridge boundaries are resolved as distinct intensity transitions (Fig. 4b) due to the differential output eliminated background signals. As shown in Fig. 4c, this operation manages to suppress nonlinear background variations and enables direct hardware-level extraction of Level 2 biometric features (bifurcations, ridge endings) and Level 3 identifiers (sweat pores)29,30. Notably, the resulting discretized edge map shows a 101% improvement in edge-specific signal-to-noise ratio, alongside 95.5% agreement with conventional digital processing outputs and higher contrast compared to conventional Sobel or Laplacian digital filters (Supplementary Fig. 23).

We also extended this in-sensor edge processing paradigm to deeper-tissue diagnostics through NIR absorption contrast. Hemoglobin in veins exhibits stronger absorption of NIR illumination than the surrounding tissues, such as skin and subcutaneous fat. NIR is thus very suitable for veins imaging. However, post-image processing techniques such as contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization and multi-scale filtering are required to address the weak contrast between the vein and surroundings tissue31–33. As shown in Fig. 4d, a photograph of a hand is provided with an inset highlighting the specific region used for imaging (Fig. 4e&f). A transmission image acquired using conventional imaging mode shows a high-intensity signal is detected between the fingers, while minimal venous detail is discernible (Fig. 4e), demonstrating the significant dynamic range challenge in conventional subcutaneous imaging. In contrast, under edge detection mode (Fig. 4f), the vein edges are clearly resolved due to abrupt transitions in hemoglobin concentration at vessel boundaries. This approach significantly enhances vein-to-tissue contrast, enabling clear visualization of vessels through differential absorption.

The device advantages for achieving this high quality image are two-fold. The intrinsically high LDR together with the differential architecture accommodate high-intensity background illumination from gap between fingers with tissue scattering and weak additive absorption signals from hemoglobin. Conventional photodetectors would otherwise saturate under high surface background intensity or lose vein-specific absorption variations in quantization noise. Consequently, the BPPU enables direct extraction of venous boundaries from raw NIR matrices without dynamic range compression. Notably, in contrast to conventional imaging with separate post-computation, our in-sensor computing approach operates at 0 V, approaching nearly zero-power data processing. Furthermore, the bipolar response characteristics of the extended BPPU array, in principle, allow it to be programmed to perform arbitrary two-dimensional linear convolution operations, effectively functioning as a versatile image processing kernel for various in-sensor computational imaging effects.

Beyond static in-sensor imaging application, the BPPU architecture also enables dynamic physiological monitoring through time-resolved differential sensing. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is a critical parameter for assessing arterial stiffness, which has been linked to various cardiovascular diseases34. Traditional PWV (𝑣) measurement requires multiple sensors and complex signal processing to analyze the time delay between pulse waves at different measurement sites35–37. However, this out- and multi-sensor data processing can be simplified by utilizing BPPU in-sensor computing. Here, we verify it through the local measurement of the fingers.

Fig. 4g schematically shows the in-sensor procession the photoplethysmographic (PPG) signal of when NIR light passes through tissues. The spatial separation (𝐷 = 2.5 mm) between the two sub-photodiodes introduces a small time lag (∆𝑇 = 𝐷/𝑣, typically < 0.5 ms for 𝑣 > 5 m s−1) in the pulse wave arriving times. This results in phase-shifted PPG signals (𝑃(𝑡) and 𝑃(𝑡−∆𝑇)) with distinct temporal characteristics. The BPPU computes the differential-delay current as 𝐼diff(𝑡) = 𝐼1(𝑡)−𝐼2(𝑡) = 𝛼[𝑃(𝑡)−𝑃(𝑡−∆𝑇)], where 𝛼 is the optoelectrical related coefficient. Since the ∆𝑇is significantly shorter than the PPG pulse wave’s characteristic timescale, the peak differential current at the maximum pulse slope ((d𝑃/d𝑡)max) is approximated by first-order Taylor expansion:
𝐼diff,max ≈ 𝛼(d𝑃/d𝑡)max ∙∆𝑇 = 𝛼(d𝑃/d𝑡)max ∙ (𝐷/𝑣) (2)

This yields the fundamental relationship of peak magnitude (𝐼diff,max) and PWV:
𝑣 = 𝑘 / 𝐼diff,max (3)

where the calibration constant 𝑘 = 𝛼 ∙𝐷(d𝑃/d𝑡)max incorporates optoelectronic and individual hemodynamic parameters. As experimentally confirmed in Fig. 4h, this inverse proportionality enables the direct translation of differential current peaks into PWV values. Fig. 4i demonstrates synchronized decreasing trends in both BPPU-derived normalized PWV and heart rate during post-exercise recovery. Physiological validation of our measurements is established through covariation with heart rate, which exhibits known correlation with PWV dynamics. Detailed signal processing is provided in Supplementary Fig. 24. Our approach thus enables efficient PWV monitoring through simple differential current measurement, offering a practical alternative to conventional multi-sensor systems.

Robust motion trajectory recognition
Finally, we use a dynamic spatiotemporal pattern recognition task to explore the potential of BPPU for intelligent vision. The task involves to identify the motion trajectory mode (32 kinds of distinct trajectories shown in Fig. 5a) of a specific target. The BPPU was scaled up to a 6×6 array. The trajectory-specific time-domain signals are generated via a convolution operation: 𝐼output(𝑡) = ∑𝑁𝑖=1 𝑅𝑖 𝜙𝑖(𝑡), where 𝑅 denotes the programmable responsivity of the 𝑖-th pixel (Fig. 3f, right), 𝜙 represents the time-dependent incident optical signal, and 𝑁 = 36 corresponds to the 6×6 array configuration. It enables the extended BPPU array directly encodes the moving objects’ spatiotemporal signatures into discriminative neuromorphic information. Or in other words, the BPPU sensor array naturally supports artificial neutral network vision processing as it played as the first layer of a neural network. The comprehensive system and detail recognition process are established in Supplementary Fig. 25 and Methods, and schematically illustrated in Fig. 5b. The original sensor output current for each BPPU in time-domain are shown in Fig. 5c & Supplementary Fig. 26. They were directly encoded into machine-readable features and sequentially fed into a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network for robust classification38,39. This workflow eliminates redundancy in conventional sensory systems (including data converters, digital edge detection, digital filtering, and optical flow calculation). Within the motion trajectory simulation platform measurements, the system achieves 100% classification accuracy across training, validation, and test sets (Fig. 5d) under noise-free conditions (Supplementary Fig. 27).

Robustness against noise is another main challenge for machine vision. We validate the system rigorous by examining its performance under perturbations. Specifically, we purposely introduced two distinct types of noise into the real trajectories: Gaussian noise and random walk noise. These were selected to simulate uncorrelated and temporally correlated interference common in real-world scenarios, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 28.

Briefly, the noises are coupled to the motion target by:
𝑥(𝑡𝑖) = 𝑥0(𝑡𝑖)+𝛼 ∙𝒩(0,𝜎2)
{ (4)

for gaussian noise, and
𝑥(𝑡𝑖) = 𝑥0(𝑡𝑖)+ 𝛼 ∑𝑖𝑘=1 𝒩(𝑘)(0,𝜎2) / 10
